overview: Apatosaurus ajax was one of the most heavily built sauropods of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, reaching 21–22 metres and 22 tonnes. Long misidentified as "Brontosaurus" — a name used for over a century before being synonymised in 1903 and partially rehabilitated in 2015 for a distinct species — Apatosaurus was a diplodocid that carried its neck horizontally and fed on low vegetation, unlike the high-browsing Brachiosaurus sharing the same ecosystem.

Its whip-like tail could potentially crack at supersonic speeds, generating a sonic boom. The neck vertebrae were massively built yet heavily pneumatised — honeycomb-like air chambers reduced the neck's mass by roughly 50% despite its enormous bulk. Apatosaurus and Diplodocus occupied different feeding zones in the same ecosystem, reducing competition despite their similar overall body plan.

articles.title: The Brontosaurus saga
articles.body: "Brontosaurus" was named by Marsh in 1879; Apatosaurus had been named by the same scientist in 1877 from a different specimen. When the two were recognised as the same genus in 1903, Apatosaurus took priority. The name Brontosaurus was used informally for decades before Emmanuel Tschopp and colleagues in 2015 demonstrated that the species previously called Brontosaurus excelsus differs enough from A. ajax to merit its own genus — so Brontosaurus is now partially rehabilitated for that species.

articles.title: Neck biomechanics
articles.body: The neck of Apatosaurus was extraordinarily thick and robust — more so than in Diplodocus for a similar body length. Air sacs inflated chambers in the vertebrae (pneumatisation), reducing mass without sacrificing structural strength. Computer models suggest the neck was carried near-horizontally rather than upright, and was used for sweeping through low-growing ferns and ground vegetation.

articles.title: Tail mechanics
articles.body: The slender whip-like distal tail has long been proposed as a "whip-crack" weapon or signalling device. Modelling by Myhrvold and Currie (1997) suggested the tail tip could reach supersonic velocities, generating a sonic boom. However, later biomechanical work argues that soft-tissue constraints — tendons, muscles, and skin — would have limited tip speed to well below the speed of sound, making a true sonic boom implausible. The tail was almost certainly used for defence or display, but the supersonic hypothesis is now contested.

fossilRecord.material: Multiple partial skeletons and substantial postcranial material from Late Jurassic quarry deposits.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Jurassic Morrison floodplains shared with Camarasaurus, Diplodocus, Stegosaurus and Allosaurus.
fossilRecord.evidence: Robust limb bones, vertebrae and tail anatomy support its heavy diplodocid body plan.

record.description: Apatosaurus was a robust diplodocid sauropod from the Morrison Formation of western North America. Multiple partial skeletons document most of the body, but skulls are rare and species-level referrals have been repeatedly revised.
facts: A. ajax is the type species; A. louisae is also widely accepted.

Brontosaurus was synonymised with Apatosaurus for much of the twentieth century, but a 2015 specimen-level analysis revived it as a separate genus; that result is influential but still tested in later work.

presentation.heroLead: A massively built, long-necked diplodocid from the Late Jurassic of western North America, known from several good skeletons but only a handful of skulls, and at the centre of the long argument over Brontosaurus.

animalParagraphs: Apatosaurus was one of the heaviest animals of the Morrison Formation, a four-legged plant-eater some twenty-one to twenty-three metres long with a deep body, a long neck of unusually broad, robust vertebrae and a whip-like tail. Mass estimates from the best skeleton cluster around sixteen to twenty-two tonnes, although any figure for a sauropod depends on the method used.

Its head was small and horse-like, with peg-shaped teeth confined to the front of the jaws, a skull type known with confidence only from a few specimens found near articulated skeletons. The neck bones carry huge downward-projecting cervical ribs, which has prompted suggestions about neck-based display or combat, but these remain hypotheses.

Two species are widely accepted, Apatosaurus ajax and A. louisae. For most of the twentieth century Brontosaurus was treated as a junior synonym, but a specimen-level analysis in 2015 argued that it is distinct; that conclusion is influential and still being tested, so the boundary between the two names is a live research question rather than settled fact.
animalHighlights: Exceptionally broad, heavily built neck vertebrae with large, downward-projecting cervical ribs.
A small, low skull with peg-like teeth restricted to the front of the mouth, known from only a few associated specimens.
A long, tapering tail ending in slender whip-like vertebrae, shared with other diplodocids.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by skull and tooth anatomy
lifeCards.reason: Peg-like teeth with wear facets indicate cropping vegetation without chewing. Feeding height and preferred plants are inferred from neck posture models, not directly preserved.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Complete limbs and girdles from several skeletons, together with Morrison sauropod trackways, establish four-legged walking. Speed is modelled, not measured.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: The near-complete A. louisae skeleton CM 3018 fixes length closely; mass depends on the reconstruction method and varies by several tonnes.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Body proportions are secure. No skin, colour or keratinous structures are known for Apatosaurus itself; small dorsal spines shown in some restorations come from an unidentified diplodocid.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Lakes' Quarry 10, near Morrison, Jefferson County, Colorado, USA

locality.name: Lakes' Quarry 10, Morrison
locality.note: Morrison Formation. The A. ajax holotype came from Arthur Lakes' excavations near Morrison; the A. louisae holotype came from the Carnegie Quarry, now Dinosaur National Monument, Utah.

presentation.classificationSummary: Apatosaurus is the name-bearing genus of Apatosaurinae within Diplodocidae. Its place among diplodocids is secure; what remains contested is how many species and genera the apatosaurine material represents, including whether Brontosaurus is separate.

related.reason: Compare with the lighter-built diplodocine that shared the Morrison floodplains.
Compare with a longer-necked diplodocid relative from the same formation.
Compare with the commonest Morrison sauropod, whose skull was once wrongly placed on Apatosaurus mounts.

questions.title: Is Brontosaurus a separate genus?
questions.copy: The 2015 specimen-level analysis by Tschopp and colleagues found enough differences to separate the two. Later studies have accepted, questioned or refined this, so the answer depends on the analysis followed.

questions.title: Which skull goes with which skeleton?
questions.copy: Only a few skulls have been found close to Apatosaurus skeletons. Historic mounts carried Camarasaurus-like skulls for decades, and some skull-to-skeleton associations remain uncertain.

questions.title: What were the huge cervical ribs for?
questions.copy: The broad, heavily built neck is unlike other diplodocids. Suggestions include neck-to-neck combat or display, but no direct evidence tests these ideas.

review.ageReviewNote: Diagnostic material is Kimmeridgian-Tithonian within the Morrison Formation.

specimens.name: Holotype of Apatosaurus ajax
specimens.note: A partial postcranial skeleton of a subadult, including neck and back vertebrae, sacrum and pelvis, collected by Arthur Lakes near Morrison, Colorado, and named by Marsh in 1877.

specimens.name: Holotype of Apatosaurus louisae
specimens.note: A nearly complete skeleton from the Carnegie Quarry, Utah, named by Holland in 1916 and mounted in Pittsburgh. A skull found nearby, CM 11162, is generally accepted as belonging to the species.

specimens.name: Referred A. louisae skeleton
specimens.institution: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County
specimens.note: A well-preserved partial skeleton with associated skull from the Carnegie Quarry, important in confirming the diplodocid-type skull of Apatosaurus.

panel.headline: Several good skeletons and a near-complete holotype, but skulls are rare.
panel.standfirst: Apatosaurus is known from multiple partial to nearly complete skeletons across Colorado, Wyoming, Utah and Oklahoma. The A. louisae holotype CM 3018 is one of the best sauropod skeletons ever found. Skull material is scarce, and which specimens belong to which species has been revised repeatedly.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is represented, most by several individuals, including a near-complete articulated skeleton; skulls are the least sampled region.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete vertebral columns from neck to tail tip, pectoral and pelvic girdles, complete fore- and hindlimbs and feet, chevrons and ribs from several skeletons, plus a small number of skulls found associated with or close to skeletons.
knownRemains.note: Because so few skulls are known and early mounts used the wrong skull, the head of Apatosaurus is reconstructed from a handful of specimens. Species assignment of many partial skeletons depends on which phylogenetic analysis is followed.

media.title: Holotype CM 3018 mounted at the Carnegie Museum
media.alt: Mounted skeleton of the Apatosaurus louisae holotype CM 3018 in the Carnegie Museum of Natural History, Pittsburgh
media.caption: The A. louisae holotype as mounted in Pittsburgh. The skeleton is largely real bone; the skull is a cast of a specimen found nearby in the same quarry.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: A few skulls with braincases and peg-like teeth, including CM 11162 and the LACM 52844 skull; most skeletons lack the head.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series in the best specimens, with the massive cervical ribs, chevrons and dorsal ribs.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete scapulocoracoids, pelves, forelimbs and hindlimbs with hands and feet from several individuals.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Bone histology has been sampled for growth studies; no skin impressions, colour or gut contents are known for Apatosaurus itself.

specimenCards.title: YPM 1860 · holotype of A. ajax
specimenCards.description: A partial skeleton of a not fully grown animal from Lakes' Quarry 10 near Morrison, Colorado, named by Marsh in 1877. Its immaturity complicated comparisons with other apatosaurines for over a century.
specimenCards.meta: Morrison, Colorado · Morrison Formation · Yale Peabody Museum

specimenCards.title: CM 3018 · holotype of A. louisae
specimenCards.description: A nearly complete articulated skeleton excavated from the Carnegie Quarry in Utah and described by Holland in 1916. It anchors most measurements of Apatosaurus size and proportions.
specimenCards.meta: Carnegie Quarry, Dinosaur National Monument, Utah · Morrison Formation · Carnegie Museum of Natural History

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Several partial to near-complete skeletons, a few associated skulls and abundant isolated bones from Morrison quarries in four states.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A heavily built, low- to mid-browsing diplodocid whose robust neck sets it apart from Diplodocus; the two apparently shared the same floodplain habitats.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Whether Brontosaurus is distinct, the function of the giant cervical ribs, habitual neck posture, precise mass and all external soft tissues.
